payload_fields.productDetailsTitle: H Frag: The Plain Fragment, and Why Its Identifiers Were Wrong Once Already
payload_fields.productDetailsDescription:
H Frag is the unmodified human growth hormone fragment spanning residues 176 to 191 — the C-terminal segment of the 191-residue hormone. Verified identifiers are molecular formula C80H127N23O24S2 and molecular weight approximately 1859.1 g/mol, recorded under PubChem CID 172966176 as HGH fragment 176-191. No CAS registry number was obtained during verification, and none is asserted here. The two sulfur atoms in the formula indicate a pair of cysteine residues.

This page has to begin with a correction, because transparency about it is more useful than a clean-looking datasheet. During verification of identifiers for this catalogue, a bulk database query for this product initially returned the record for AOD9604 — molecular formula C78H123N23O23S2, molecular weight approximately 1815.1 g/mol. That result was wrong. AOD9604 is a *modified* analogue of this fragment, not the fragment itself, and the two differ by roughly 44 g/mol: identical nitrogen and sulfur counts, differing by two carbons, four hydrogens and one oxygen. The error was caught by checking the returned record against the compound actually being looked up, and corrected to CID 172966176.

Recording that matters for a practical reason. If an automated lookup silently substitutes the modified analogue's record for the plain fragment's, then any datasheet, listing or certificate assembled by automated lookup is liable to carry the same substitution. A document headed "HGH Fragment 176-191" quoting a molecular weight of 1815.1 is describing AOD9604, whatever its title says. Checking the quoted figure against the two values — 1859.1 for the plain fragment, 1815.1 for AOD9604 — detects this immediately, and is worth doing on any document accompanying either product.

The relationship between the two compounds also determines what evidence applies to this one, and here the honest answer is unflattering. The pharmacological rationale for this fragment class is that growth hormone's lipolytic activity — its promotion of fat breakdown — may reside in a discrete portion of the molecule, separable from the hormone's growth-promoting and glucose-metabolic effects. A fragment retaining the first while shedding the others would be a more targeted agent than the hormone. That hypothesis is coherent and was taken seriously enough to support a pharmaceutical development programme.

But that programme used the modified analogue, not the plain fragment. When a 2006 review of obesity drugs in clinical development covered this compound class, the compound it named was AOD-9604 (PMID 16625817). The modification exists precisely because the plain fragment was judged insufficient as a drug candidate — which is the usual reason a developer modifies a lead compound rather than taking it forward unchanged. So the clinical development history that is commonly invoked for "HGH fragment" belongs to a different molecule, and that molecule's programme itself produced no published efficacy result and no approved product, as the AOD9604 page in this catalogue sets out.

The position for this product is therefore straightforward and should not be dressed up: no completed clinical trial of the plain hGH 176-191 fragment was identified in the indexed literature. The mechanistic hypothesis is interesting, the modified analogue derived from it reached the clinic and did not emerge, and the plain fragment has less evidence behind it than the analogue does.

A naming note. This compound appears as H Frag, HGH Frag 176-191, HGH fragment 176-191, hGH 176-191, and sometimes simply as "fragment" or "frag". AOD9604 is the modified analogue and a distinct molecule. Somatropin, recombinant human growth hormone, is the full 191-residue protein, is an approved medicine for defined indications, and bears no useful resemblance to a 16-residue fragment in size, properties or regulatory status — the shared "growth hormone" terminology is the only thing connecting them.

The material is supplied as a lyophilised powder in a sealed glass vial. The stated quantity refers to the mass of material in the vial. Lyophilised peptides are hygroscopic, so the usual laboratory convention is to allow a sealed vial to reach room temperature before opening it, so that atmospheric moisture does not condense onto cold powder. Amino Based publishes no product-specific stability study for this material, so no shelf-life, reconstituted-stability or freeze-thaw tolerance figures are claimed here; where such data are needed for a protocol they should be established in the receiving laboratory or taken from a lot-specific certificate. This product is supplied in a nominal 5 mg presentation.
payload_fields.researchFocusTitle: A Hypothesis Worth Testing, With the Evidence Attached to a Different Molecule
payload_fields.researchFocusDescription:
The research position for the plain fragment is best described by separating three things that marketing routinely merges: the biology of growth hormone, the development history of the modified analogue, and the evidence for this specific peptide.

The biology of growth hormone is well established and not in dispute. Growth hormone is a 191-residue protein with a broad range of effects: it promotes linear growth and tissue anabolism largely through induction of insulin-like growth factor 1, it influences glucose metabolism in ways that can oppose insulin action, and it promotes lipolysis in adipose tissue. That breadth is exactly what makes the whole hormone unsuitable as a weight-loss agent — the metabolic and growth-promoting effects come along with the lipolytic one.

The structure-activity hypothesis follows naturally and is genuinely interesting: if the lipolytic activity maps to a discrete region of the molecule, a peptide comprising only that region might reproduce fat breakdown without the rest. This is a legitimate question in peptide pharmacology, and it has real precedent in both directions. Elsewhere in this catalogue, KPV — a three-residue fragment of a thirteen-residue hormone — retains an anti-inflammatory effect while shedding the parent's pigmentation activity, demonstrating that selectivity-by-truncation can work. Other fragments fail to reproduce their parents' effects, or act by different mechanisms. Which outcome applies to a given fragment is an empirical question that cannot be settled by reasoning from the parent hormone.

For this fragment, that empirical question has not been answered in the published literature. No completed clinical trial of the plain hGH 176-191 fragment was identified in the indexed record.

What exists instead is the development history of the modified analogue, and the way that history bears on this product is worth spelling out because the inference usually runs the wrong way. When a 2006 review surveyed obesity compounds in clinical development, the fragment-class entry was AOD-9604 — the modified molecule (PMID 16625817). A developer who modifies a lead compound and takes the modified version into trials is, by that act, indicating that the unmodified version was judged inadequate: typically for stability, potency, or pharmacokinetic reasons. So the existence of AOD9604 is itself weak evidence *against* the plain fragment being the better candidate, rather than evidence in favour of fragments generally.

And the modified analogue's own history is not a success story. No publication reporting a completed AOD9604 efficacy trial appears in the indexed literature, the compound is approved nowhere, and secondary sources report that its phase IIb trial failed to separate from placebo and that the programme was terminated in 2007. The full chain is therefore: an interesting hypothesis, a plain fragment judged insufficient to develop, a modified analogue developed instead, and that analogue discontinued without a published positive result. Material promoting the plain fragment on the strength of "clinical research into HGH fragments" is drawing on that chain while omitting how it ends.

The limitations, stated plainly: there is no clinical trial evidence for this specific peptide; the development-stage evidence concerns a different molecule; that molecule's programme produced no published efficacy result and no approval; and the fragment-retains-parent-activity assumption is a hypothesis rather than a finding for this particular fragment.

For a laboratory, this nonetheless describes a reasonable and tractable piece of work rather than a dead end. The structure-activity question is real, and this catalogue happens to contain both members of the relevant comparison pair — the plain fragment and the modified analogue — with a defined 44 g/mol structural difference and readily distinguishable masses. Comparative lipolysis assays in adipocyte culture, run on correctly identified material from both vials with appropriate controls, would address directly what two decades of marketing has asserted without evidence: whether either fragment does what the parent hormone's lipolytic activity would suggest, and whether the modification makes a difference. That is a well-posed experiment with a clear readout, and it is more interesting than the compound's commercial narrative.
payload_fields.qualityPurityTitle: Analytical Verification: Confirming This Is Not the Other Fragment
payload_fields.qualityPurityDescription:
Amino Based publishes analytical results on a per-lot basis. Where a lot-specific certificate of analysis has been issued for this product it is available from the Certificates page, and any purity figure displayed on this page is taken directly from that certificate and stated exactly as recorded. Where no certificate has been published for a lot, no analytical result is claimed for it here, and the absence of a figure should be read as the absence of a published measurement rather than as an implied standard.

Identity confirmation is against the verified molecular formula C80H127N23O24S2 and molecular weight of approximately 1859.1 g/mol (PubChem CID 172966176). No CAS registry number was obtained during verification, so a certificate quoting a CAS number for this compound should be checked rather than assumed — and in particular, a certificate quoting CAS 221231-10-3 is quoting AOD9604's registry number, which identifies a different molecule.

The primary check is discrimination from AOD9604, and it is reassuringly simple. The modified analogue is approximately 1815.1 g/mol; this fragment is approximately 1859.1. A difference of about 44 g/mol, roughly 2.4 per cent, is comfortably resolved by ordinary intact mass spectrometry at this mass. So a certificate that reports an observed mass numerically settles the question outright. Conversely, a certificate that reports only a purity percentage and a compound name establishes nothing about which of the two molecules is present — and given that an automated lookup for this product returned the wrong record during verification of this catalogue, the possibility of a document describing the wrong molecule is demonstrated rather than hypothetical.

Disulfide integrity is the second check. The formula contains two sulfur atoms, indicating two cysteine residues. Reduction of a disulfide adds two hydrogens, so the reduced form is heavier by only 2 mass units out of 1,859 — about 0.1 per cent, well within the tolerance of a loosely specified intact-mass measurement. Where the bridged form is intended, confirming it requires accurate mass with the 2-unit distinction explicitly addressed, a free-thiol assay such as Ellman's reagent, or chromatographic separation of reduced from oxidised forms. The companion question is dimerisation: a free thiol on one molecule can pair with another to give intermolecular disulfide dimers at roughly twice the monomer mass, which are not detected by a purity figure reported without reference to the high-mass region.

Sequence confirmation by tandem mass spectrometry fragmentation is worth requesting. At around 16 residues, a single-residue substitution or deletion is a small proportional mass change, and sequence data is what distinguishes a correct preparation of this fragment from a related fragment of different boundaries. Fragments are defined by their residue range, and a preparation spanning slightly different residues would be a different peptide.

Purity assessment by reverse-phase chromatography is appropriate, and the impurity classes to expect are deletion sequences, truncated chains, the reduced monomer, and disulfide dimers. Because the related marketed compound differs by a structural modification, the presence of modified material within a plain-fragment preparation is also a plausible cross-contamination route where a supplier produces both.

The salt-form question applies as usual, and lyophilised mass is not peptide content: a vial labelled 5 mg may contain counter-ions and residual water, and unless content has been determined specifically, the stated figure is a fill mass.

Amino Based has not performed independent laboratory testing, manufacturing validation, or primary research on this compound beyond what is recorded on any published lot certificate, and makes no claim of third-party accreditation, pharmaceutical-grade manufacture, or regulatory approval for this product.
payload_fields.complianceNoticeTitle: Research Use Only: No Trial Evidence, and a Development History Belonging to Another Molecule
payload_fields.complianceNoticeDescription:
This product is supplied for laboratory research use only (RUO). It is not for human or veterinary use. It is not a drug, a dietary supplement, a cosmetic, a food or a medical device, and it must not be used in the diagnosis, treatment, cure, mitigation or prevention of any disease or condition in humans or animals. Sale is restricted to qualified researchers, laboratories and scientific institutions. Nothing on this page constitutes medical advice, and no administration, dosing or reconstitution guidance for human or veterinary use is provided here or available on request.

H Frag is not an approved medicine. The human growth hormone fragment 176-191 has not been approved by the United States Food and Drug Administration or by any other regulatory authority, for any indication, in any jurisdiction. There is no regulator-reviewed labelling, no approved indication, no established dosing, and no post-marketing safety surveillance. No completed clinical trial of this fragment was identified in the PubMed-indexed literature.

One point of attribution requires emphasis, because claims about this product routinely borrow evidence that does not belong to it. The clinical development history commonly invoked for "HGH fragment" concerns AOD9604, a *modified* analogue and a chemically distinct molecule approximately 44 g/mol lighter. When a 2006 review surveyed obesity compounds then in clinical development, the compound it named in this class was AOD-9604, not the plain fragment. The existence of that modified analogue indicates that the unmodified fragment was judged insufficient to develop, which is the ordinary reason a developer modifies a lead rather than advancing it unchanged. And the analogue's own programme produced no published efficacy result and no approved product, with secondary sources reporting that its phase IIb trial failed to separate from placebo and that development ended in 2007.

So the chain of evidence invoked for this product is: an interesting structure-activity hypothesis, a plain fragment not taken into development, a modified analogue developed in its place, and that analogue discontinued without a published positive result. Material promoting this fragment on the strength of clinical research into growth hormone fragments is relying on that chain while omitting its conclusion.

A further point concerns the parent hormone. Recombinant human growth hormone, somatropin, is an approved medicine for defined indications. It is a 191-residue protein, and a 16-residue fragment of it is a different substance with different properties and no approval anywhere. Nothing about somatropin's regulatory status or clinical evidence transfers to this material.

Nothing on this page suggests that this material is suitable for addressing obesity, weight loss, body composition, fat metabolism, growth disorders or any other condition in any person. It is not for human use.

Researchers remain responsible for compliance with the law in their own jurisdiction, for institutional review and biosafety approvals where their work requires them, for any import and export controls applying to shipments of research chemicals, and for safe handling and disposal of the material. Labelling a substance "research use only" describes the supplier's intended use and the terms of sale; it is not a determination of legal status and does not exempt a purchaser from applicable law.

Standard institutional practice for handling lyophilised peptide powders applies: appropriate personal protective equipment, handling in a suitable containment environment to avoid aerosolising fine powder, and disposal of vials and residual solutions in accordance with institutional chemical and biohazard waste protocols.
